Figure 1:Two observations motivatingGRAPE-Bench.(a) Model rankings change between driving videos with synthetic rain and footage captured in real rain. Among the five models shown, MiniCPM-V 4.5 drops from first to third, while Cosmos-Reason2 rises from third to first.
(b) Three questions about the same rainy driving scene illustrate why greater difficulty need not imply greater safety relevance. Identifying whether the ego vehicle stopped for a red light (L1) and reasoning about a two-wheeler’s motion relative to its original lane (L2) both receive high safety relevance scores. Counting the vehicles initially queued on the left (L3) is the hardest question, answered incorrectly by 90% of the evaluated models, yet receives a safety relevance score of 38.

Table 2:Results on theGRAPE-Benchsynthetic set.Accuracy (%; higher is better) under twelve visual corruptions. Driving reports L1–L3 separately; daily-life columns (Avg.) pool questions across levels, and All pools questions across all levels and corruptions.Δ\Deltais synthetic minus clean All accuracy (pp) on the same questions. Shading indicates1st,2nd, and3rdplace per column.

Table 3:Results on theGRAPE-Benchreal-world set.Accuracy (%; higher is better) on driving videos captured under naturally occurring rain, snow, nighttime, and fog conditions. L1–L3 are reported separately for each condition, and each condition’s Avg. pools its questions across all levels. Rank orders models by decreasing All Avg. (1 is best). Rank and top-3 shading are computed separately for proprietary and open-source VLMs. Fine-tuned variants use Qwen3.5-9B and the synthetic training split only (Section4).

Figure 3:Synthetic question construction inGRAPE-Bench.Sampled frames provide scene context and question-relevant evidence for generating L1–L3 questions, reference answers, and distractors. Candidates undergo six verification gates.
